journeyIntro: For understanding how you show up with others. Practise awareness, honest needs and steadier responses.

lessons.title: Notice Your Signals
lessons.summary: Spot what happens before you react.

steps.title: Your body speaks first
steps.body: A tight jaw, a hot face, a sinking feeling. Your body often notices tension before your mind does, and those signals are useful early warnings.

steps.prompt: A colleague asks for a favour and you feel a flash of irritation. What’s the most helpful first move?

options.text: Pause and ask yourself: am I tired, rushed or just not willing?
options.why: Naming what’s behind the irritation helps you answer honestly instead of on autopilot.

options.text: Say yes straight away, then resent it.
options.why: Ignoring the signal often turns into resentment that leaks out later.

options.text: Snap “I’m busy” before you’ve thought about it.
options.why: The irritation is valid, but a reflex reply can sting more than you meant it to.

steps.prompt: Name it to yourself.
steps.why: Naming your own state, not their fault, is the first step to a calmer reply.

steps.prompt: Where do you first notice stress in your body?
steps.reply: That’s your early-warning signal. Spotting it gives you a second to choose your response.

steps.prompt: Match each body signal with what it might mean.
steps.why: Your body often notices feelings before your mind does. Spotting the signal gives you time to choose a response.

steps.body: Before replying to your next request, notice and name one feeling to yourself first.

lessons.title: Name the Feeling
lessons.summary: More words for feelings means more choices.

steps.title: “Fine” hides a lot
steps.body: Many of us only use “fine”, “stressed” or “angry”. Finding a more precise word, like disappointed, left out or overwhelmed, helps you understand what you need, and calms the feeling too.

steps.prompt: Your friend cancelled plans and you feel “annoyed”. Which word might describe it more precisely?

options.text: “Fine.”
options.why: It hides the feeling, which makes it harder to know what you need.

options.text: “Disappointed. I was really looking forward to it.”
options.why: A precise word points to what matters to you, so you can respond well.

options.text: “Furious.”
options.why: Possibly, but it may be bigger than what you actually feel.

steps.prompt: Be more precise.
steps.after: by how much is on my plate.
steps.why: The right word tells you what kind of help you need.

steps.prompt: Which feeling word do you use most?
steps.reply: Next time, try asking yourself: what’s underneath that word?

steps.prompt: Match each general word with a more precise one.
steps.why: Precise feeling words make it easier to understand yourself and ask for what you need.

steps.body: Three times today, pause and find a more precise word for how you feel.

lessons.title: Feelings Have Messages
lessons.summary: Each feeling is telling you something.

steps.title: Feelings are information
steps.body: Feelings aren’t good or bad. Anger often signals a crossed line, sadness a loss, anxiety something that matters. Asking “what is this telling me?” turns a feeling into useful information.

steps.prompt: You feel anxious every Sunday evening before the work week. What might it be telling you?

options.text: Something about the week ahead needs attention or support.
options.why: Treating anxiety as a message helps you find what to change or plan.

options.text: You’re just a worrier.
options.why: A label stops you looking at what the feeling is pointing to.

options.text: Nothing. Ignore it and it’ll go.
options.why: Ignored feelings tend to come back louder.

steps.prompt: Ask the feeling.
steps.why: Getting curious about a feeling helps you respond instead of react.

steps.prompt: Which feeling do you find hardest to sit with?
steps.reply: Getting curious about it, gently, can make it feel less overwhelming.

steps.prompt: Listening to a feeling, or pushing it away?

cards.text: “Why am I so on edge today?”
Talking it through with a friend

steps.why: Listening to feelings helps you understand and meet your needs. Pushing them away usually makes them stronger.

steps.body: Next time a strong feeling shows up, ask: “What is this telling me?” and write the answer down.

lessons.title: Listen to Understand
lessons.summary: Notice when your mind is preparing a defence.

steps.title: The defence lawyer in your head
steps.body: When someone suggests you could do something differently, your mind may start building a case before they’ve finished. Noticing that is a skill.

steps.prompt: Someone close to you suggests you’ve been a bit distant lately. What’s the most helpful response?

options.text: Build your rebuttal while they’re still talking.
options.why: You’ll respond to what you feared they’d say, and miss what they actually meant.

options.text: Decide they’re attacking who you are.
options.why: Treating one observation as a verdict on you makes it much harder to hear.

options.text: “Can you tell me more about what you’ve noticed?”
options.why: Curiosity helps you understand what they mean before deciding whether you agree.

steps.title: Hearing isn’t agreeing
steps.body: You can fully understand someone’s view and still see it differently. Listening first just means your reply is to what they really said.

steps.prompt: Get curious instead.
steps.why: An open question slows things down and helps you hear the real point.

steps.prompt: Which kind of comment makes you most defensive?
steps.reply: Knowing your sore spot helps you catch the defence early and stay curious.

steps.prompt: Understanding or defending?

cards.text: “Can you tell me more about that?”
“When did it start to feel that way?”
“That makes sense. Thanks for saying it.”

steps.why: Understanding means getting curious about their view first; defending can wait, and often isn’t needed at all.

steps.body: Next time you feel criticised, ask one clarifying question before defending yourself.

lessons.title: Stay Present
lessons.summary: Listen to them, not your next reply.

steps.title: Your mind races ahead
steps.body: While others talk, many of us are planning what to say next. Gently bringing your attention back to their words, again and again, is what real listening feels like.

steps.prompt: A friend is telling you about their week, and you notice you’re planning your own story. What do you do?

options.text: Keep planning so you’re ready to share.
options.why: You’ll miss what they’re saying, and they may notice.

options.text: Gently bring your attention back to their words.
options.why: Noticing and returning is the core skill of listening.

options.text: Interrupt with your story before you forget.
options.why: It takes the moment away from them.

steps.prompt: Come back to them.
steps.before: When my mind drifts, I gently
steps.why: Returning, without judging yourself, gets easier the more you practise.

steps.prompt: Where does your mind go when others talk?
steps.reply: Noticing where it goes is the first step to bringing it back.

steps.prompt: Staying present. Put these in order.
steps.why: Noticing and returning keeps you present; a follow-up question shows you were truly listening.

steps.body: In your next conversation, notice when your mind drifts and gently bring it back.

lessons.title: Hear Your Inner Voice
lessons.summary: Notice how you talk to yourself.

steps.title: You’re always listening to you
steps.body: We all have an inner voice running commentary. Often it’s far harsher than we’d ever be to a friend. Simply noticing what it says is the first step to changing it.

steps.prompt: You forget a friend’s birthday. Your inner voice says, “You’re useless, you always mess up.” What’s the healthiest response?

options.text: Agree with it. You did mess up.
options.why: One slip doesn’t make you useless. Harsh self-talk only adds hurt.

options.text: Notice it, then say: “I forgot, and I can make it right.”
options.why: You acknowledge the slip kindly and move to fixing it.

options.text: Ignore it and distract yourself.
options.why: The voice tends to return. Answering it kindly works better.

steps.prompt: Talk to yourself like a friend.
steps.before: What would I say to a
steps.why: Most of us are far kinder to friends. Turning that kindness inward helps.

steps.prompt: When do you notice your inner critic most?
steps.reply: Knowing when it shows up helps you get ready with a kinder reply.

steps.prompt: Inner critic, or kind inner voice?

cards.text: “That was hard, and you did your best.”

steps.why: A kind inner voice doesn’t ignore mistakes. It helps you learn from them without tearing you down.

steps.body: Today, catch one harsh thought about yourself and rewrite it as you would for a friend.

lessons.title: Know Your Needs
lessons.summary: Your needs deserve clear words.

steps.title: You can’t ask for what you can’t name
steps.body: Many of us are better at sensing what others need than our own needs. Knowing yours, like rest, space or reassurance, makes them easier to ask for.

steps.prompt: You’re exhausted after a long week, and a friend invites you to another party tonight. What’s healthiest?

options.text: Check your energy honestly, and kindly decline if you need rest.
options.why: Listening to your needs helps you show up better for friends when you do go.

options.text: Go anyway because you’d feel guilty saying no.
options.why: Guilt-driven yeses can leave you drained, distracted and a little resentful.

options.text: Say yes, then cancel at the last minute.
options.why: Last-minute cancellations hurt more than an honest no would have.

steps.prompt: Say it kindly.
steps.before: I’d love to, but I need
steps.why: Naming your need simply and warmly makes a no easy for others to accept.

steps.prompt: Which need of yours often goes unspoken?
steps.placeholder: I often need… but don’t say it.

steps.prompt: Working out what you need. Put these in order.
steps.why: You can’t ask for a need you haven’t named. Feeling first, then need, then words makes asking much easier.

steps.body: Name one need to yourself today, then act on it kindly, even in a small way.

lessons.title: Rest Without Guilt
lessons.summary: Rest isn’t lazy. It’s how you recharge.

steps.title: Rest is productive
steps.body: Many people feel guilty resting while there’s still more to do. But there will always be more to do. Rest is what lets you show up well for yourself and others.

steps.prompt: It’s Saturday, you’re exhausted, and there’s still housework to do. What’s healthiest?

options.text: Push through it all, then crash.
options.why: Running on empty tends to lead to burnout.

options.text: Rest guilt-free for the morning, then do the most important job.
options.why: Rest first, then a realistic task, helps you recover and still get things done.

options.text: Rest, but feel bad the whole time.
options.why: Guilt stops rest from actually recharging you.

steps.prompt: Give yourself permission.
steps.after: even when there’s more to do.
steps.why: Permission to rest is what turns downtime into real recovery.

steps.prompt: What helps you truly rest?
steps.reply: Plan a little of that this week, and notice how it changes your energy.

steps.prompt: Match each guilty thought with a kinder one.

pairs.b: “Rest isn’t a reward, it’s a need.”

steps.why: Kinder thoughts let you rest properly, so you come back with more energy.

steps.body: Schedule thirty minutes of guilt-free rest this week and protect it.

lessons.title: People-Pleasing
lessons.summary: You can be kind without always saying yes.

steps.title: Pleasing everyone costs you
steps.body: Saying yes to keep everyone happy can leave you drained and resentful. Noticing the urge to please, and pausing before you answer, helps you choose what you really want.

steps.prompt: A neighbour asks you to water their plants for two weeks while you’re very busy. Your instinct is to say yes. What’s best?

options.text: Say yes. You don’t want them to think badly of you.
options.why: Agreeing out of fear often leads to stress and resentment.

options.text: Avoid them until they ask someone else.
options.why: Avoidance can feel awkward and leaves them waiting.

options.text: “Let me check my diary and get back to you tonight.”
options.why: A pause gives you time to decide what you can genuinely offer.

steps.prompt: Buy yourself time.
steps.why: A short pause breaks the automatic yes, so you can choose freely.

steps.prompt: Who do you find it hardest to say no to?
steps.reply: Practising a pause with that person first can make a big difference.

steps.prompt: People-pleasing, or healthy kindness?

cards.text: Apologising for things that aren’t your fault
“I can’t this time, but good luck!”
Hiding your opinion to avoid conflict

steps.why: Healthy kindness comes from choice, not fear. You can care about others and still look after yourself.

steps.body: Next time someone asks you for something, pause before answering, even for a moment.

lessons.title: Notice Connection Bids
lessons.summary: Your attention can build closeness.

steps.title: Small moments, every day
steps.body: People reach for connection in small ways: sharing news, a joke, a sigh. How you usually respond shapes how close people feel to you.

steps.prompt: Someone you care about texts you some small good news while you’re busy. What builds closeness?

options.text: Reply with a thumbs-up without really reading it.
options.why: Quick reactions are fine sometimes, but often they can feel like you didn’t notice.

options.text: Take a moment to celebrate, and ask a question about it.
options.why: A few seconds of real interest tells them their good moments matter to you.

options.text: Reply with your own news instead.
options.why: Sharing is good, but leading with yours can make their moment feel brushed aside.

steps.prompt: Respond to the bid.
steps.why: A follow-up question invites them to share more and enjoy the moment with you.

steps.prompt: When do you most often miss people’s bids?
steps.reply: That’s your moment to watch for. Even a short, warm reply makes a difference.

steps.title: An old photo

lines.text: Found it clearing out Mum’s loft.

steps.prompt: It’s you both on a camping trip. Reply:

options.text: Haha yeah
options.why: A flat reply turns away from a bid, and they may stop reaching out.

options.text: No way, the tent that collapsed in the rain! 😂 We should go again this summer.
options.reaction: YES. Without the rain this time 😂
options.why: You shared the memory and built on it, turning a small bid into a real moment together.

options.text: (You leave it on read and reply tomorrow.)
options.why: Missing small bids is easy, but they’re how closeness grows or quietly fades.

steps.body: Respond fully to one small moment of connection today, even if it only takes a minute.

lessons.title: Be the One Who Reaches Out
lessons.summary: Don’t wait to be invited.

steps.title: Everyone is waiting for someone
steps.body: Many people feel lonely while waiting for others to make the first move. Reaching out first, a text, an invite, a call, often gets a warm response, because they were waiting too.

steps.prompt: You’ve been feeling a bit lonely lately. What’s a good first step?

options.text: Message a friend: “Fancy a walk this weekend?”
options.why: A simple, specific invite is an easy way to reconnect.

options.text: Wait for someone to notice and get in touch.
options.why: Others may be busy or waiting for you too.

options.text: Post a sad status online.
options.why: It may get likes, but a direct message brings real connection.

steps.prompt: Make it easy.
steps.why: A light, specific invite is easy to say yes to.

steps.prompt: Who could you reach out to this week?
steps.reply: One message is all it takes to start.

steps.prompt: Reaching out. Put these in order.
steps.why: One person and one small plan make reaching out feel manageable, and following up shows you mean it.

steps.body: Reach out to one person today with a simple invitation.

lessons.title: Make Time for People
lessons.summary: Relationships need a place in your week.

steps.title: Busy weeks squeeze out people
steps.body: Work and chores fill every gap if you let them. Putting time with people in your diary, like any other appointment, makes sure connection doesn’t keep getting pushed back.

steps.prompt: You keep saying you’ll see friends “when things calm down”. What’s most likely to help?

options.text: Wait until you’re less busy.
options.why: Busy seasons often roll into each other, so “later” rarely comes.

options.text: Book one regular catch-up a week, like Thursday dinner.
options.why: A regular slot means connection happens, even in busy times.

options.text: Plan one big catch-up every few months.
options.why: Nice, but small, regular contact keeps you closer.

steps.prompt: Put it in the diary.
steps.why: Protecting a regular time makes connection a habit, not an afterthought.

steps.prompt: How much of your week goes to people you love?
steps.reply: Even one protected hour a week can change how connected you feel.

steps.title: A gentle nudge

lines.text: We keep saying we’ll catch up 😅
Life is so busy right now!

steps.prompt: Reply:

options.text: I know! Let’s do it when things calm down.
options.why: It sounds friendly, but “when things calm down” often never comes.

options.text: Let’s just book it! Thursday at 7, our usual spot?
options.why: Turning “we should” into a booked plan makes it actually happen.

options.text: Tell me about it, I’m swamped.
options.why: Agreeing about being busy keeps you stuck in the same pattern.

steps.body: Book one regular time with someone you care about, and put it in your diary.

lessons.title: Keep Promises to Yourself
lessons.summary: Build confidence through doable commitments.

steps.title: Self-trust works like any trust
steps.body: Each time you break a promise to yourself, you trust yourself a little less. Each small promise kept rebuilds it, so start tiny.

steps.prompt: You keep promising yourself an hour of journalling every day, and it never happens. What’s the best next step?

options.text: Promise two hours tomorrow to make up for it.
options.why: Bigger promises after slips usually lead to more slips, and more self-criticism.

options.text: Swap it for five minutes a day, which you know you’ll manage.
options.why: A small promise you keep builds momentum and self-trust far better than a big one you don’t.

options.text: Decide you just can’t stick to anything.
options.why: That story is unkind and untrue; the plan was too big, not you too weak.

steps.prompt: Make it small enough.
steps.why: Small enough to do on a bad day is the secret to keeping it every day.

steps.prompt: Which promise to yourself do you break most often?
steps.reply: Make that promise smaller, then keep it. Self-trust grows from there.

steps.prompt: Realistic, or all-or-nothing?

cards.text: “An hour every day, starting today, forever”
“I missed a day, so I’ve failed”
“I missed a day, so I’ll start again tomorrow”
Linking it to something you already do

steps.why: Small, specific promises you can keep build self-trust; perfect plans tend to break and leave you feeling worse.

steps.body: Choose one tiny commitment to yourself today, and keep it exactly as planned.

lessons.title: Tiny Habits
lessons.summary: Start so small you can’t fail.

steps.title: Small habits stick
steps.body: Big goals often fail because they need too much willpower. A tiny version, two minutes of stretching, one line in a journal, is easy to keep, and keeping it builds trust in yourself.

steps.prompt: You want to read more but never seem to find time. Which plan is most likely to stick?

options.text: Read for an hour every night from tonight.
options.why: Ambitious, but one busy evening can break the habit.

options.text: Read when you feel like it.
options.why: Without a plan, it’s easy to keep putting off.

options.text: Read one page in bed every night.
options.why: So small it’s easy to keep, and it often grows naturally.

steps.prompt: Link it to something.
steps.before: After I brush my teeth, I’ll
steps.why: Linking a new habit to an existing one makes it much easier to remember.

steps.prompt: Which habit would you like to build?
steps.reply: What’s the tiniest version of it you could start today?

steps.prompt: Match each big goal with a tiny first step.
steps.why: Tiny steps you actually take build trust in yourself, and often grow into bigger habits.

steps.body: Choose one habit and start the tiniest possible version of it today.

lessons.title: Kindness After Slips
lessons.summary: Missing a day doesn’t undo your progress.

steps.title: Slips are part of change
steps.body: Everyone misses a day, breaks a streak or falls back into an old habit. What matters is how you respond. Kindness helps you get back on track; harshness makes you want to give up.

steps.prompt: You’ve kept up your morning walks for three weeks, then missed four days. What’s the best response?

options.text: “I’ve failed. There’s no point now.”
options.why: All-or-nothing thinking throws away three weeks of progress.

options.text: “I missed a few days. Tomorrow I’ll walk again.”
options.why: Kind and practical, which helps you restart without drama.

options.text: Double the walks to make up for it.
options.why: Punishing yourself makes the habit feel like a chore.

steps.prompt: Start again.
steps.why: Seeing slips as normal makes it much easier to keep going.

steps.prompt: When you slip up on a goal, you usually…
steps.reply: Starting again quickly, with kindness, is the habit that matters most.

steps.prompt: Kind response, or harsh?
steps.why: Kind responses keep you moving. Harsh ones make you want to stop altogether.

steps.body: Next time you slip on a goal, say one kind sentence to yourself and restart the next day.

lessons.title: Pause Before Reacting
lessons.summary: Give yourself room to choose a response.

steps.title: The space between
steps.body: Between something happening and how you respond, there’s a small space. Widening it, even by a few breaths, gives you a choice.

steps.prompt: A message from a friend reads as rude, and you’re itching to fire back. What’s the most helpful move?

options.text: Send the first sharp reply that comes to mind.
options.why: Reactive replies are hard to take back and can start a row over a misunderstanding.

options.text: Wait a bit, reread it, and ask what they meant if it’s still unclear.
options.why: Messages lose tone; a pause and a question often reveal it wasn’t meant how it sounded.

options.text: Assume they meant to hurt you.
options.why: Assuming the worst makes it harder to respond fairly, even if they were just rushed.

steps.title: Three breaths is enough
steps.body: Breathe in slowly, breathe out longer, three times. It calms your body’s alarm so you can answer with the part of you that thinks clearly.

steps.prompt: Check before reacting.
steps.before: Not sure how to read this.
steps.why: A simple question gives them a chance to clarify before anything escalates.

steps.prompt: Pausing before you react. Put these in order.
items: Ask what else it could mean
steps.why: A short pause gives your thinking brain time to catch up, so you respond the way you’d actually want to.

steps.body: Before your next difficult reply, take three slow breaths and reread what they actually said.

lessons.title: Name It to Tame It
lessons.summary: Saying what you feel helps it settle.

steps.title: Naming calms the storm
steps.body: When a strong feeling hits, simply naming it, “I’m feeling really frustrated right now”, helps your brain settle. It creates a little space between the feeling and what you do next.

steps.prompt: Your partner forgets to pick up the shopping, again. You feel a surge of frustration. What helps first?

options.text: Say exactly what you’re thinking, straight away.
options.why: In the heat of the moment, words often come out harsher than you mean.

options.text: Silently say to yourself, “I’m frustrated,” and take a breath.
options.why: Naming the feeling calms it, so you can respond rather than react.

options.text: Pretend it doesn’t bother you.
options.why: Pushing feelings down tends to make them burst out later.

steps.prompt: Name it.
steps.why: Putting a feeling into words gives you a moment of calm and choice.

steps.prompt: Which feeling most often makes you react quickly?
steps.reply: Naming that one feeling when it shows up can change how you respond.

steps.prompt: When a strong feeling hits. Put these in order.
items: Notice the feeling in your body
steps.why: Noticing and naming come before choosing, which is what makes a calm response possible.

steps.body: Next time you feel a strong emotion, name it silently before you say anything.

lessons.title: Handle Criticism Calmly
lessons.summary: Take what’s useful, leave the rest.

steps.title: Criticism stings, but can help
steps.body: Hearing criticism can feel like an attack. Pausing, asking a question and taking what’s useful, while letting go of what isn’t, keeps you calm and helps you grow.

steps.prompt: A friend tells you that you can come across as dismissive in group chats. It stings. What’s best?

options.text: “That’s not true, you’re being oversensitive.”
options.why: Defending straight away means you miss what could be useful.

options.text: Go quiet and feel hurt for days.
options.why: Stewing keeps the sting without the learning.

options.text: “That’s hard to hear, but thanks for telling me. Can you give me an example?”
options.why: Calm and curious, so you can understand and decide what to change.

steps.prompt: Get curious.
steps.why: A concrete example helps you see what they mean, so you can respond fairly.

steps.prompt: How do you usually react to criticism?
steps.reply: Whatever your habit, a pause and one question can change how it goes.

steps.prompt: Match each defensive reaction with a calmer one.
steps.why: Calm responses let you learn from criticism without losing your sense of self-worth.

steps.body: Next time you receive criticism, ask one curious question before you respond.

lessons.title: Own Your Part
lessons.summary: Responsibility is different from self-blame.

steps.title: Responsibility, not shame
steps.body: Owning your part means saying, “I did that, and I’ll do better.” Shame says, “I’m terrible.” The first helps relationships; the second just hurts you.

steps.prompt: You realise you interrupted a friend several times while they were telling you something important. What now?

options.text: “I keep cutting you off, I’m sorry. Please finish.”
options.why: It owns the behaviour simply and gives the moment back to them.

options.text: Tell yourself you’re a terrible friend.
options.why: Harsh self-talk doesn’t help them, and it makes it harder to change next time.

options.text: “You were taking ages to get to the point.”
options.why: Explaining why they made you do it shifts blame and adds hurt to the moment.

steps.prompt: Own it, kindly.
words: am the worst at listening to
steps.why: Naming the action, not condemning yourself, keeps the repair simple and sincere.

steps.prompt: When you make a mistake with someone, what do you tend to do?
steps.reply: Whatever your pattern, aim for simple ownership: what you did, and what you’ll do next.

steps.title: A hard thing to hear

lines.text: Can I be honest? Sometimes it feels like our chats are all about you.
I don’t want to fight about it.

steps.prompt: It stings. What do you say?

options.text: Ouch, but thank you for telling me. Can you tell me when it felt like that?
options.reaction: Thanks for taking it well. Like last week, at the café…
options.why: You stayed open even though it hurt, which is how you learn your part and keep the friendship.

options.text: That’s not fair. I always ask about you!
options.reaction: See, this is what I mean…
options.why: Arguing the point proves theirs and makes it harder for them to be honest again.

options.text: Sorry. I’m a terrible friend.
options.why: Putting yourself down shifts the focus to your feelings instead of what they shared.

steps.body: Notice one small mistake with someone today and repair it in a sentence, without blaming you or them.

lessons.title: Apologise Well
lessons.summary: A clear apology heals faster than excuses.

steps.title: A real apology has no “but”
steps.body: A good apology names what you did, acknowledges how it affected them and says what you’ll do differently. No excuses, and no “sorry if you were upset”.

steps.prompt: You snapped at your flatmate after a stressful day. Which apology is best?

options.text: “I snapped at you, and that wasn’t fair. Sorry. Next time I’ll say I’m stressed.”
options.why: It owns the action, the impact and the change, without excuses.

options.text: “Sorry, but I’ve had a terrible day.”
options.why: The “but” turns the apology into an excuse.

options.text: “Sorry if you were upset.”
options.why: It puts the problem on their feelings, not your action.

steps.prompt: Drop the excuse.
steps.why: Saying it wasn’t fair shows you understand the impact on them.

steps.prompt: What makes apologising hardest for you?
steps.reply: Knowing what holds you back makes it easier to apologise sooner.

steps.prompt: Real apology, or a non-apology?
steps.why: Real apologies take responsibility and look forward. Non-apologies quietly shift the blame.

steps.body: If you owe someone an apology, give it this week, with no “but”.

lessons.title: Forgive Yourself
lessons.summary: Learn from mistakes without carrying them forever.

steps.title: Guilt can help, shame doesn’t
steps.body: Guilt says “I did something wrong”, and can help you make amends. Shame says “I am bad”, and just weighs you down. Forgiving yourself means learning the lesson and letting the weight go.

steps.prompt: Months ago, you said something hurtful to a friend. You apologised and they forgave you, but you still feel awful. What helps?

options.text: Keep going over it so you never do it again.
options.why: Replaying it doesn’t make you kinder, it just keeps you hurting.

options.text: “I made a mistake, I made amends, and I’ve learnt from it. I can let this go.”
options.why: You honour the lesson and release the shame.

options.text: Avoid the friend so you don’t feel bad.
options.why: Avoidance can damage a friendship that’s already been repaired.

steps.prompt: Let it go.
steps.before: I’ve learnt from it, and I can
steps.why: Letting go after making amends lets you move forward as a kinder person.

steps.prompt: Is there something you’re still holding against yourself? What did you learn from it?
steps.placeholder: e.g. I learnt to pause before I reply

steps.prompt: Forgiving yourself. Put these in order.
steps.why: Owning it and learning from it come first. Then letting go becomes possible, and healthy.

steps.body: Write down one mistake you’ve learnt from, and one kind sentence to let it go.

lessons.title: Question Your Story
lessons.summary: Separate what happened from what you assume.

steps.title: Facts and stories
steps.body: “They haven’t replied” is a fact. “They’re angry with me” is a story. Our minds blend the two so quickly that the story feels like the fact.

steps.prompt: A friend hasn’t replied to your message all day, and you’re starting to feel anxious. What’s most helpful?

options.text: Decide they’re upset with you.
options.why: Treating the story as fact can lead you to act on something that isn’t true.

options.text: Send several messages asking why they’re ignoring you.
options.why: If they’re simply busy, a flurry of messages can create the tension you feared.

options.text: Notice the fact, then think of a few other reasons they might not have replied.
options.why: Holding several explanations loosens the grip of the worst one and calms you down.

steps.prompt: Separate fact from story.
steps.before: They haven’t replied yet. They might
steps.why: A neutral explanation is often the most likely one, and the easiest to live with.

steps.prompt: Think of a worry about someone. What’s the fact, and what’s the story?
Match each anxious story with a kinder one.

pairs.b: “I can just ask if we’re okay.”

steps.why: Anxious stories feel like facts but are guesses. A kinder, likely story calms you enough to check what’s true.

steps.body: Next time you’re worried about someone, write down one fact and two other possible explanations.

lessons.title: The Comparison Trap
lessons.summary: Comparing your inside to their highlight reel.

steps.title: Comparison steals joy
steps.body: Scrolling through others’ holidays, promotions and perfect homes, it’s easy to feel behind. But you’re comparing your whole life to their best moments. Your path is your own.

steps.prompt: You see an old classmate’s post about buying a big house, and feel like a failure. What’s the healthiest thought?

options.text: “I’m so far behind everyone.”
options.why: One post isn’t the full story, of their life or yours.

options.text: “Good for them. My life has its own good things and its own timing.”
options.why: You can be happy for them while staying grounded in your own path.

options.text: Unfollow everyone who seems successful.
options.why: Sometimes helpful, but the comparison habit can follow you.

steps.prompt: Compare with yourself.
steps.before: Compared to a year ago, I’ve
steps.why: Comparing with your past self shows real progress that others can’t see.

steps.prompt: What do you compare yourself on most?
steps.reply: Noticing your trigger helps you catch the comparison before it takes over.

steps.prompt: Match each comparison with a grounding thought.
steps.why: Grounding thoughts bring you back to your own life, where your real progress is.

steps.body: When you catch yourself comparing today, name one thing you’re proud of in your own life.

lessons.title: Inner Critic, Inner Coach
lessons.summary: Turn harsh self-talk into encouragement.

steps.title: Swap the critic for a coach
steps.body: A critic tears you down; a coach is honest but helps you improve. Asking “What would a good coach say here?” turns harsh self-talk into something useful.

steps.prompt: You stumble over your words in a presentation. Your inner voice says, “You embarrassed yourself.” What would a coach say?

options.text: “You’re right, that was awful.”
options.why: That’s the critic again, and it doesn’t help you improve.

options.text: “Who cares, it doesn’t matter.”
options.why: Brushing it off skips a chance to learn.

options.text: “You recovered well. Next time, a bit more practice on the opening.”
options.why: Honest, kind and useful, which is exactly what a good coach does.

steps.prompt: Coach yourself.
steps.why: A coach focuses on what to do next, not on what went wrong.

steps.prompt: Who has been a great coach or mentor in your life?
steps.reply: Imagining what they’d say can help you talk to yourself more kindly.

steps.title: Your inner voice

lines.text: You forgot to reply to Sam AGAIN.

steps.prompt: Answer like a coach:

options.text: You’re right. I’m hopeless.
options.reaction: (You feel worse, and still don’t reply.)
options.why: Agreeing with the critic makes you feel worse and doesn’t fix anything.

options.text: I slipped up, but I care about Sam. I’ll reply now and set a reminder.
options.reaction: (You send the message and feel lighter.)
options.why: Coach-style talk owns the slip and moves you to action.

options.text: It doesn’t matter, Sam won’t notice.
options.why: Brushing it off leaves the problem, and the feeling, unresolved.

steps.body: When your inner critic speaks today, answer it the way a kind coach would.

lessons.title: Ask for What Helps
lessons.summary: Make your requests clear and manageable.

steps.title: People can’t read minds
steps.body: Hoping others will notice you’re struggling often leads to feeling let down. A clear, small request gives people who care a way to help.

steps.prompt: You’re overwhelmed and wish someone would help, but nobody seems to notice. What’s the best next step?

options.text: Wait and hope someone notices.
options.why: Others may be busy or unsure; waiting can leave you struggling alone for longer.

options.text: Drop hints, then feel hurt when they miss them.
options.why: Hints are easy to miss, and the hurt can come out sideways in other ways.

options.text: Ask someone you trust for one specific kind of help.
options.why: A specific ask is easy to say yes to, and you get the help you actually need.

steps.prompt: Make one specific ask.
steps.after: on Thursday? It would really help.
steps.why: One clear, doable request is much easier to agree to than a vague cry for help.

steps.title: Bigger support is okay too
steps.body: If you’ve been feeling low or overwhelmed for a while, talking to a doctor, counsellor or support line can help. Asking for that is a strength.

steps.title: Someone notices

lines.text: You okay? You’ve seemed really stressed this week.

steps.prompt: You are, and you could use help. Reply:

options.text: I’m fine, don’t worry about me!
options.why: Brushing off an offer of care means you stay overwhelmed and they can’t help.

options.text: Ugh, everything is just too much.
options.reaction: Oh no. Anything I can do?
options.why: Honest, but without a clear ask it’s hard for them to know how to help.

options.text: Thanks for asking. Honestly, I’m swamped. Could you cook tonight? I’ll do Friday.
options.why: You accepted the care and made a small, clear ask, which is easy for someone to say yes to.

steps.body: Make one clear, small request for support this week from someone you trust.

lessons.title: Accept Help
lessons.summary: Letting others help is a gift to them too.

steps.title: Receiving is a skill
steps.body: Many people are great at helping and terrible at being helped. Saying “Thank you, that would be great” instead of “No, I’m fine” lets others show they care, and lightens your load.

steps.prompt: You’re recovering from flu. A friend offers to drop off soup. Your instinct is to say you’re fine. What’s best?

options.text: “Honestly, that would be lovely. Thank you!”
options.why: Accepting graciously lets them help and lets you rest.

options.text: “No, no, I don’t want to be a bother.”
options.why: Refusing can leave them feeling shut out.

options.text: Accept, then apologise repeatedly.
options.why: Over-apologising can make kindness feel like a burden.

steps.prompt: Accept graciously.
steps.why: A simple, warm yes makes helping you feel good to them.

steps.prompt: What makes accepting help hard for you?
steps.reply: Remember how good it feels to help someone you care about. They feel the same.

steps.prompt: Accepting help, or pushing it away?

cards.text: “Yes please, could you grab some milk?”
Letting a friend cook for you

steps.why: Accepting help deepens relationships. It shows trust, and lets others care for you as you care for them.

steps.body: The next time someone offers help, say yes and thank them.

lessons.title: Your Support Circle
lessons.summary: Know who you can turn to, for what.

steps.title: Different people, different support
steps.body: No one person can meet all your needs. One friend is great for practical help, another for a laugh, another for deep talks. Knowing your circle helps you reach the right person.

steps.prompt: You’re worried about a big decision and want someone to talk it through with. What’s the best approach?

options.text: Keep it to yourself so you don’t burden anyone.
options.why: Big decisions are easier with support, and people often want to help.

options.text: Ask the friend who’s thoughtful and a good listener.
options.why: Choosing the right person for the kind of support you need makes it far more helpful.

options.text: Ask everyone you know for their opinion.
options.why: Too many views can make it more confusing.

steps.prompt: Reach the right person.
steps.why: Knowing who’s good for what helps you get the right support quickly.

steps.prompt: Who would you turn to for practical help, a laugh, or a deep talk?
steps.placeholder: e.g. practical: Dad, laugh: Jess, deep talk: Amir

steps.prompt: Match each need with the kind of person to ask.
steps.why: Spreading your needs across a circle of people makes support easier to find and to give.

steps.body: Write down your support circle, and reach out to one person in it this week.

lessons.title: Choose Your Next Step
lessons.summary: Turn insight into one sustainable habit.

steps.title: From noticing to doing
steps.body: You’ve learned a lot about your patterns. Real change rarely comes from big resolutions; it comes from one small habit, repeated.

steps.prompt: You’ve noticed you pull away from people when you’re stressed. What’s the most realistic next step?

options.text: Promise to always be there for everyone.
options.why: It sounds generous, but it’s impossible to keep and sets you up to feel you’ve failed.

options.text: Pick one simple check-in, like a weekly call with a close friend.
options.why: A small, regular habit keeps you connected even on stressful weeks.

options.text: Wait until life calms down to reconnect.
options.why: Life rarely calms down on its own, and connection helps you cope while it’s busy.

steps.prompt: Which pattern of yours would you most like to shift?
steps.reply: That’s a great focus. One small habit aimed at it, kept for a few weeks, can really change things.

steps.prompt: What one small habit will you practise next week?
Pulling away, or reaching out?

cards.text: Muting the group chat for a week
Telling one person how you really are
Replying to a message you’ve been avoiding

steps.why: Stress pulls us inward; small steps towards people, even one message, help you feel less alone in it.

steps.body: Pick one small relationship habit to practise every day next week, and put a reminder somewhere you’ll see it.

lessons.title: Celebrate Small Wins
lessons.summary: Notice your progress, however small.

steps.title: Small wins add up
steps.body: It’s easy to only notice what’s still left to do. Pausing to notice small wins, a hard conversation handled, a habit kept, builds confidence and motivation to keep going.

steps.prompt: This week you finally told a friend how you really felt about something. What’s the best response?

options.text: Move straight on. It was nothing special.
options.why: Skipping the win means missing a chance to build confidence.

options.text: Focus on what you could have said better.
options.why: Reflection is useful, but first, notice what you did well.

options.text: Take a moment to feel proud, and tell someone close.
options.why: Celebrating helps the new habit stick, and shares the good moment.

steps.prompt: Notice it.
steps.why: Naming your pride turns a small moment into lasting motivation.

steps.prompt: What’s one small win from this week?
steps.reply: Whatever it is, it counts. Give yourself credit for it.

steps.prompt: Celebrating a win, or brushing it off?

cards.text: Writing it in a wins list

steps.why: Celebrating small wins builds confidence. Brushing them off makes progress feel invisible.

steps.body: Start a short wins list today, and add one thing to it.

lessons.title: Keep Growing
lessons.summary: Growth is a practice, not a finish line.

steps.title: You’ll keep learning
steps.body: Better relationships come from small skills, practised again and again. You won’t get it perfect, and you don’t need to. Choosing one thing to keep practising is what makes the change last.

steps.prompt: You’ve finished this journey. What’s the best way to keep growing?

options.text: Try to practise everything at once.
options.why: Too much at once is hard to keep up.

options.text: Pick one skill to focus on this month.
options.why: One focused skill is easier to practise until it becomes natural.

options.text: Assume you’re done now.
options.why: Skills fade without practice. Keeping one going keeps you growing.

steps.prompt: Choose your focus.
steps.why: Naming one skill to practise turns learning into lasting change.

steps.prompt: Which skill do you most want to keep practising?
steps.reply: That’s a great choice. Small, steady practice is what makes it stick.

steps.prompt: Keeping a skill going. Put these in order.
steps.why: One skill at a time, practised often, is how lasting growth happens.

steps.body: Choose one skill from this journey to practise every day this month.
